source_refs.note: Exercise 4.2, Question 2: Without expansion show ten determinant results, parts (i)-(x) (book pages 58-59).

blocks.explanation:
A "without expansion" proof: we may only use properties of determinants.
We must show the value is 0, so we aim for two identical columns or a zero column.
Plan: subtract \(C_1\) from \(C_2\) and \(C_3\); then compare the new columns.
steps:
Given: \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 7 & 8 & 9 \\ 5 & 6 & 7 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix}\)
To prove: \(\Delta = 0\) without expanding.
Method: Property vii (subtracting one column from another keeps the value), Property v (common factor out), Property iii (two identical columns give 0). The columns \(7, 8, 9\) etc. increase by 1, which suggests subtracting.

Subtract column 1 from columns 2 and 3
\[C_2 - C_1 \to C_2,\quad C_3 - C_1 \to C_3\]
\[\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 7 & 1 & 2 \\ 5 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: \(8 - 7 = 1,\ 6 - 5 = 1,\ 3 - 2 = 1\) and \(9 - 7 = 2,\ 7 - 5 = 2,\ 4 - 2 = 2\). By Property vii the value does not change.

Take 2 out of column 3
\[\Delta = 2\begin{vmatrix} 7 & 1 & 1 \\ 5 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: Every entry of \(C_3\) is 2 (Property v).

Identical columns
\[\Delta = 2 \times 0 = 0\]
Why: Property iii: a determinant with two identical columns (or rows) is zero. Here \(C_2 = C_3\).

Check (only to confirm; the proof above needs no expansion)
\[7(24 - 21) - 8(20 - 14) + 9(15 - 12)\]
\[= 21 - 48 + 27 = 0 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Expanding along row 1 gives the same result.

blocks.explanation:
A "without expansion" proof; the value must come out 0.
We look for a combination of columns that becomes all zeros.
Plan: notice that \(C_3 = C_1 - C_2\); so \(C_3 - C_1 + C_2\) is a zero column.
steps:
Given: \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 5 & 6 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -8 & 10 \end{vmatrix}\)
To prove: \(\Delta = 0\) without expanding.
Method: Property vii (adding multiples of columns to another column keeps the value) and Property iv (a column of zeros gives 0). Spot the relation: row 1: \(5 - 6 = -1\); row 2: \(2 - 2 = 0\); row 3: \(2 - (-8) = 10\). So each entry of \(C_3\) equals (entry of \(C_1\)) \(-\) (entry of \(C_2\)).

Subtract \(C_1\) from \(C_3\) and add \(C_2\) to it
\[C_3 - C_1 + C_2 \to C_3\]
\[\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 5 & 6 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -8 & 0 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: Row 1: \(-1 - 5 + 6 = 0\); row 2: \(0 - 2 + 2 = 0\); row 3: \(10 - 2 - 8 = 0\). This is two Property vii steps, so the value is unchanged.

A zero column
\[\Delta = 0\]
Why: Property iv: if all entries of a column are zero, the determinant is zero (expanding along that column gives \(0 + 0 + 0\)).

Check (only to confirm)
\[5(20 - 0) - 6(20 - 0) + (-1)(-16 - 4)\]
\[= 100 - 120 + 20 = 0 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Expansion along row 1 agrees.

blocks.prompt: 2 (iii) Without expansion show that: \(\begin{vmatrix} -a & 0 & b \\ 0 & a & -c \\ c & -b & 0 \end{vmatrix} = 0\)
blocks.explanation:
A "without expansion" proof with letters; the value must be 0.
We look for a combination of rows that gives a zero row.
Plan: multiply \(R_3\) by \(a\), then add \(c R_1\) and \(b R_2\) to it.
steps:
Given: \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} -a & 0 & b \\ 0 & a & -c \\ c & -b & 0 \end{vmatrix}\)
To prove: \(\Delta = 0\) without expanding.
Method: Property v (multiplying a row by \(a\) multiplies the determinant by \(a\)), Property vii (adding multiples of rows keeps the value), Property iv (zero row gives 0). First take \(a \neq 0\).

Multiply \(R_3\) by \(a\)
\[\Delta = \dfrac{1}{a}\begin{vmatrix} -a & 0 & b \\ 0 & a & -c \\ ac & -ab & 0 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: Multiplying a row by \(a\) multiplies the value by \(a\), so we put \(\frac{1}{a}\) outside to keep the value the same.

Add \(cR_1\) and \(bR_2\) to \(R_3\)
\[R_3 + cR_1 + bR_2 \to R_3\]
\[\Delta = \dfrac{1}{a}\begin{vmatrix} -a & 0 & b \\ 0 & a & -c \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: Column 1: \(ac - ac + 0 = 0\); column 2: \(-ab + 0 + ab = 0\); column 3: \(0 + bc - bc = 0\). Property vii keeps the value.

A zero row
\[\Delta = \dfrac{1}{a} \times 0 = 0\]
Why: Property iv.

The case \(a = 0\)
\[\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 & b \\ 0 & 0 & -c \\ c & -b & 0 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: If \(b \neq 0\), multiply \(R_2\) by \(b\) and add \(cR_1\): \(R_2\) becomes \((0, 0, -bc + bc) = (0, 0, 0)\), so \(\Delta = 0\). If \(b = 0\) too, \(R_1\) is already a zero row. So \(\Delta = 0\) in every case.

Check (only to confirm)
\[-a(0 - bc) - 0 + b(0 - ac)\]
\[= abc - abc = 0 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Expansion along row 1 agrees.

blocks.prompt: 2 (iv) Without expansion show that: \(\begin{vmatrix} l & m+n & 1 \\ m & n+l & 1 \\ n & l+m & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0\)
blocks.explanation:
A "without expansion" proof; the value must be 0.
Adding \(C_1\) to \(C_2\) gives \(l + m + n\) in every row of \(C_2\).
Plan: \(C_2 + C_1 \to C_2\), take \(l + m + n\) out, compare \(C_2\) and \(C_3\).
steps:
Given: \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} l & m+n & 1 \\ m & n+l & 1 \\ n & l+m & 1 \end{vmatrix}\)
To prove: \(\Delta = 0\) without expanding.
Method: Property vii, Property v, Property iii. Each row of \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) together contains all three letters \(l, m, n\).

Add column 1 to column 2
\[C_2 + C_1 \to C_2\]
\[\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} l & l+m+n & 1 \\ m & l+m+n & 1 \\ n & l+m+n & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: \(l + (m+n)\), \(m + (n+l)\), \(n + (l+m)\) are all \(l + m + n\). Property vii keeps the value.

Take \(l + m + n\) out of column 2
\[\Delta = (l+m+n)\begin{vmatrix} l & 1 & 1 \\ m & 1 & 1 \\ n & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: Property v.

Identical columns
\[\Delta = (l+m+n) \times 0 = 0\]
Why: Property iii: a determinant with two identical columns (or rows) is zero. Here \(C_2 = C_3\).

blocks.explanation:
A "without expansion" proof; the value must be 0.
Column 3 is \(3x, 9x, 15x\): all multiples of \(3x\).
Plan: take \(3x\) out of \(C_3\), then compare \(C_2\) and \(C_3\).
steps:
Given: \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3x \\ 2 & 3 & 9x \\ 3 & 5 & 15x \end{vmatrix}\)
To prove: \(\Delta = 0\) without expanding.
Method: Property v (common factor out of a column) and Property iii (identical columns).

Take \(3x\) out of column 3
\[\Delta = 3x\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & 5 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: \(3x = 3x \cdot 1\), \(9x = 3x \cdot 3\), \(15x = 3x \cdot 5\).

Identical columns
\[\Delta = 3x \times 0 = 0\]
Why: Property iii: a determinant with two identical columns (or rows) is zero. Here \(C_2 = C_3\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (vi) Without expansion show that: \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & p^2 & \frac{p}{qr} \\ 1 & q^2 & \frac{q}{rp} \\ 1 & r^2 & \frac{r}{pq} \end{vmatrix} = 0\)
blocks.explanation:
A "without expansion" proof with fractions; the value must be 0.
The fractions in \(C_3\) can all be written over the same denominator \(pqr\).
Plan: rewrite \(C_3\), take \(\frac{1}{pqr}\) out, compare \(C_2\) and \(C_3\).
steps:
Given: \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & p^2 & \frac{p}{qr} \\ 1 & q^2 & \frac{q}{rp} \\ 1 & r^2 & \frac{r}{pq} \end{vmatrix}\), with \(p, q, r \neq 0\).
To prove: \(\Delta = 0\) without expanding.
Method: Make the denominators equal (multiply top and bottom), then Property v and Property iii.

Rewrite column 3 over \(pqr\)
\[\dfrac{p}{qr} = \dfrac{p \cdot p}{qr \cdot p} = \dfrac{p^2}{pqr}\]
\[\dfrac{q}{rp} = \dfrac{q^2}{pqr},\quad \dfrac{r}{pq} = \dfrac{r^2}{pqr}\]
Why: Multiplying the top and bottom of a fraction by the same non-zero number does not change it.

Take \(\frac{1}{pqr}\) out of column 3
\[\Delta = \dfrac{1}{pqr}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & p^2 & p^2 \\ 1 & q^2 & q^2 \\ 1 & r^2 & r^2 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: Property v.

Identical columns
\[\Delta = \dfrac{1}{pqr} \times 0 = 0\]
Why: Property iii: a determinant with two identical columns (or rows) is zero. Here \(C_2 = C_3\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (vii) Without expansion show that: \(\begin{vmatrix} p-q & q-r & r-p \\ q-r & r-p & p-q \\ r-p & p-q & q-r \end{vmatrix} = 0\)
blocks.explanation:
A "without expansion" proof; the value must be 0.
In every row the three entries add up to 0.
Plan: \(C_1 + C_2 + C_3 \to C_1\) gives a zero column.
steps:
Given: \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} p-q & q-r & r-p \\ q-r & r-p & p-q \\ r-p & p-q & q-r \end{vmatrix}\)
To prove: \(\Delta = 0\) without expanding.
Method: Property vii (add columns into one) and Property iv (zero column).

Add all columns into column 1
\[C_1 + C_2 + C_3 \to C_1\]
\[\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 0 & q-r & r-p \\ 0 & r-p & p-q \\ 0 & p-q & q-r \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: Row 1: \((p - q) + (q - r) + (r - p) = 0\); rows 2 and 3 have the same three brackets in another order, so they also give 0.

A zero column
\[\Delta = 0\]
Why: Property iv: a column of zeros makes the determinant zero.

blocks.prompt: 2 (viii) Without expansion show that: \(\begin{vmatrix} yz & zx & xy \\ x & y & z \\ \frac{1}{x} & \frac{1}{y} & \frac{1}{z} \end{vmatrix} = 0\)
blocks.explanation:
A "without expansion" proof; the value must be 0.
Multiplying column 1 by \(x\), column 2 by \(y\), column 3 by \(z\) makes row 1 all \(xyz\) and row 3 all 1.
Plan: do that, take \(xyz\) out of \(R_1\), compare \(R_1\) and \(R_3\).
steps:
Given: \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} yz & zx & xy \\ x & y & z \\ \frac{1}{x} & \frac{1}{y} & \frac{1}{z} \end{vmatrix}\), with \(x, y, z \neq 0\).
To prove: \(\Delta = 0\) without expanding.
Method: Property v (used both ways: multiplying a column by \(k\) multiplies the value by \(k\)) and Property iii (identical rows).

Multiply \(C_1\) by \(x\), \(C_2\) by \(y\), \(C_3\) by \(z\)
\[\Delta = \dfrac{1}{xyz}\begin{vmatrix} xyz & xyz & xyz \\ x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: \(yz \cdot x = xyz\), \(zx \cdot y = xyz\), \(xy \cdot z = xyz\); \(\frac{1}{x} \cdot x = 1\) and so on. The value was multiplied by \(xyz\), so we divide by \(xyz\) outside.

Take \(xyz\) out of row 1
\[\Delta = \dfrac{xyz}{xyz}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ x^2 & y^2 & z^2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: Property v.

Identical rows
\[\Delta = 1 \times 0 = 0\]
Why: Property iii: here \(R_1 = R_3\), so the determinant is zero.

blocks.prompt: 2 (ix) Without expansion show that: \(\begin{vmatrix} bc & a & a^2 \\ ca & b & b^2 \\ ab & c & c^2 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a^2 & a^3 \\ 1 & b^2 & b^3 \\ 1 & c^2 & c^3 \end{vmatrix}\)
blocks.explanation:
A "without expansion" proof that two determinants are equal.
The right side has a column of 1s and the powers \(a^2, a^3\); the left side has \(bc, a, a^2\).
Plan: multiply \(R_1, R_2, R_3\) by \(a, b, c\); then \(C_1\) becomes \(abc\) in every row.
steps:
Given: left side \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} bc & a & a^2 \\ ca & b & b^2 \\ ab & c & c^2 \end{vmatrix}\), with \(a, b, c \neq 0\).
To prove: \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a^2 & a^3 \\ 1 & b^2 & b^3 \\ 1 & c^2 & c^3 \end{vmatrix}\) without expanding.
Method: Property v, used to multiply rows and then to take a common factor out of a column.

Multiply \(R_1\) by \(a\), \(R_2\) by \(b\), \(R_3\) by \(c\)
\[\Delta = \dfrac{1}{abc}\begin{vmatrix} abc & a^2 & a^3 \\ abc & b^2 & b^3 \\ abc & c^2 & c^3 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: \(bc \cdot a = abc\), \(a \cdot a = a^2\), \(a^2 \cdot a = a^3\), and similarly in rows 2 and 3. The value was multiplied by \(abc\), so we divide by \(abc\) outside.

Take \(abc\) out of column 1
\[\Delta = \dfrac{abc}{abc}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & a^2 & a^3 \\ 1 & b^2 & b^3 \\ 1 & c^2 & c^3 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{vmatrix} 1 & a^2 & a^3 \\ 1 & b^2 & b^3 \\ 1 & c^2 & c^3 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: Property v; \(\frac{abc}{abc} = 1\). This is exactly the right side.
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: the two determinants are equal.

blocks.prompt: 2 (x) Without expansion show that: \(\begin{vmatrix} 2a & a+b & a+c \\ 2b & 2b & b+c \\ 2c & b+c & 2c \end{vmatrix} = 0\)
blocks.explanation:
A "without expansion" proof; the value must be 0.
Column 1 is \(2a, 2b, 2c\); half of it is \(a, b, c\).
Plan: subtract \(\frac{1}{2}C_1\) from \(C_2\) and \(C_3\); then take \(b\) and \(c\) out.
steps:
Given: \(\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 2a & a+b & a+c \\ 2b & 2b & b+c \\ 2c & b+c & 2c \end{vmatrix}\)
To prove: \(\Delta = 0\) without expanding.
Method: Property vii (subtract a multiple of a column), Property v (common factor), Property iii (identical columns).

Subtract half of column 1 from columns 2 and 3
\[C_2 - \tfrac{1}{2}C_1 \to C_2,\quad C_3 - \tfrac{1}{2}C_1 \to C_3\]
\[\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 2a & b & c \\ 2b & b & c \\ 2c & b & c \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: New \(C_2\): \((a+b) - a = b\), \(2b - b = b\), \((b+c) - c = b\). New \(C_3\): \((a+c) - a = c\), \((b+c) - b = c\), \(2c - c = c\). Property vii keeps the value.

Take \(b\) out of \(C_2\) and \(c\) out of \(C_3\)
\[\Delta = bc\begin{vmatrix} 2a & 1 & 1 \\ 2b & 1 & 1 \\ 2c & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: Property v.

Identical columns
\[\Delta = bc \times 0 = 0\]
Why: Property iii: a determinant with two identical columns (or rows) is zero. Here \(C_2 = C_3\).
